name: Gold Foil
basis: why: foil laid on card wherever a heated die touches; how: threshold mask as the die, crumpled foil reflecting a strip

lumenary.blurb: Metal foil stamped onto card where your picture is bright, crumpled into a thousand tiny mirrors.

facts.era: Gold leaf is ancient, hot stamping from the 19th century

why: Foil stamping lays a thin metal film on card wherever a heated die touches it. Here your picture is the die: foil goes where the picture is bright. Crumpled foil is a field of tiny creases, each facing a different way, and so each catches a different part of the room, which is why foil sparkles.
how: Decide where foil goes with a smoothstep around a threshold, given a slightly ragged edge by a little noise.
Show the card’s own colour and a fine grain everywhere else.
Build a crumpled height map from ridged noise at three scales, with a slow warp so the creases wander.
Read the up and down tilt of each facet to choose a colour from a strip that stands for what a metal sheet reflects.
Add a thin brighter rim along the edge of the stamped area.
history: Gold leaf has decorated manuscripts, icons and temples for thousands of years. Hot foil stamping, pressing metallic film onto a surface with a heated die, developed with industrial printing and now decorates book covers, wedding invitations and packaging. The ridged noise behind the crumple was popularised by the graphics researcher Ken Musgrave.
terms: Pressing a thin metal film onto a surface with a heated die.
Noise folded so that its middle value becomes a sharp crease.
One small flat panel of a faceted surface.
paragraphs: Foil stamping lays a thin metal film onto card wherever a heated die touches it. Here the die is your picture: the foil goes where the picture is bright (or, with the toggle, where it is dark). Coverage is a smoothstep around a threshold set by the coverage slider, with a ragged edge from a little noise, so the boundary looks torn, not cut. The rest of the card shows its own colour with fine grain.

Foil is crumpled, so its surface is a field of creases. The program builds a height map from ridged noise, the function 1 − |2n − 1| of smooth noise, which has sharp creases where the noise crosses its middle value, at three scales (the finer two weighted less) and bends the coordinates with a slow warp so the creases wander. The slope gives a normal, and the up-and-down tilt picks a position on a strip of colours that stands for what a metal sheet reflects: dark at the edges, bright in the middle. Each tiny panel therefore flashes a different tone. A thin brighter rim is added along the edge of the stamped area.

equations.note: Foil coverage c; ρ is a small noise that roughens the edge.
Crumple height from ridged noise R; f₀ = 1.5 × the facet slider ÷ the picture width.
Position on the foil’s colour strip from the tilt (n_x, n_y) of the normal and the picture brightness.

presets.text: Rose foil on dark ink card is elegant and modern.
Heavy crumple with small facets makes a glittering sheet.
Stamp the dark parts instead of the bright ones.
